findings.antecedent: Binaural listening (both ears having similar sensitivity)
findings.quote: The binaural thresholds of hearing shown in Figure 11-1 and Table 11-1 are approximately 2 dB lower than the corresponding monaural thresholds if both ears have similar sensitivity

findings.antecedent: Increasing frequency (below 500 Hz)
findings.quote: The audibility of low frequency stimuli improves with increasing frequency at an average rate of about 12 dB/octave

findings.antecedent: Aging (from 20 to 70 years of age, at frequencies above 8,000 Hz)
findings.quote: The typical changes in the threshold of hearing with age, from 20 to 70 years of age, at frequencies above 8,000 Hz, exceed 60 dB in normally hearing population.

findings.antecedent: Acoustic resonances of the ear canal and concha
findings.consequent: Auditory system sensitivity (in 3.0 to 4.0 kHz range)
findings.quote: The high sensitivity of the auditory system in this frequency range results from acoustic resonances of the ear canal and concha

findings.antecedent: Occluding the ear canal by an earphone
findings.consequent: Amplification of low frequency physiologic noise and elevation of MAP threshold
findings.quote: occluding the ear canal by an earphone was reported to cause an amplification of low frequency physiologic noise (e.g., blood flow noise) by the closed cavity of the ear canal and elevation of MAP threshold at low frequencies

findings.antecedent: Background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range)
findings.quote: the threshold of discomfort is almost independent of background noise level (in 30 to 70 dB SPL range) and exceeds 80 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: Sound pressure level increase of about 10 dB (for 1-kHz tone at moderate and high intensity levels)
findings.quote: for moderate and high intensity levels the loudness of a 1-kHz tone doubles when its sound pressure level increases by about 10 dB

findings.antecedent: Neurophysiologic hearing loss
findings.quote: individuals with neurophysiologic hearing loss have elevated thresholds of hearing but still have about the same or even lower threshold of pain. These shifts in thresholds result in a narrower dynamic range of hearing

findings.antecedent: Sound duration (for sounds shorter than critical duration)
findings.quote: for sounds shorter than critical duration, the loudness of sound increases with sound duration

findings.antecedent: Higher repetition rate and shorter duration of clicks or noise bursts
findings.quote: bursts of higher repetition rate and shorter duration have been reported to sound louder than the same bursts of longer duration and slower repetition rate

findings.antecedent: Sustained, fixed-level, auditory stimulation
findings.quote: Auditory adaptation, or loudness adaptation, is a gradual decrease in hearing sensitivity during sustained, fixed-level, auditory stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Increasing frequency (for auditory adaptation)
findings.quote: The amount of adaptation is dependent on the frequency, level and duration of the auditory stimulus and increases with decreasing level of the stimulus and increasing frequency

findings.antecedent: Excessive exposure to sounds energy (2000 to 6000 Hz)
findings.quote: Excessive exposure to sounds energy in the frequency range from 2000 to 6000 Hz is most likely to cause permanent changes in hearing.

findings.antecedent: Masker intensity (in simultaneous masking)
findings.quote: the masked threshold increases about 10 dB for every 10 dB increase in masker.

findings.antecedent: Bandwidth of narrowband masker (up to critical band limits)
findings.quote: As the bandwidth of the narrowband masker increases, its masking effectiveness increases until its bandwidth exceeds the limits of the critical band

findings.antecedent: Simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands
findings.quote: simultaneous presence of signal energy in several critical bands aids signal detection.

findings.antecedent: Time difference between offsets of masker and target sound (forward masking)
findings.quote: Masking decreases as the intensity of the masker decreases, the separation between the sounds increases, and the time difference between the two offsets increases.

findings.antecedent: Similarity between the masker and the target sound
findings.quote: Two main causes of informational masking are similarity between the masker and the target sound and the variability (uncertainty) of the masker

findings.antecedent: Spatial uncertainty regarding the location of the masker
findings.quote: it has been shown that uncertainty of the spatial position of the masker can reduce speech intelligibility of the speech target... or detection of the nonspeech target

findings.antecedent: Aging (even with normal hearing, in presence of informational maskers)
findings.quote: older individuals (age 60 or greater) performed as well as younger individuals in speech recognition in an energetic masking background but performed much poorer in the presence of informational maskers.

findings.antecedent: Frequency separation between individual tones of a sound (smaller than critical band)
findings.quote: Dissonance occurs if the frequency separation between the individual tones of the sound is smaller than a critical band with its maximum for tones separation equal about ¼ of the critical band

findings.antecedent: Increased sound intensity (for higher frequencies)
findings.quote: for tones of higher frequencies, increased sound intensity produces an increase in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Increased sound intensity (for lower frequencies)
findings.quote: Conversely, for tones of lower frequencies, increased sound intensity produces a decrease in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Dynamically changing sound intensity (Doppler illusion)
findings.quote: listeners perceived the rising sound intensity as an upward shift in pitch.

findings.antecedent: Frequency components separated by more than one critical band
findings.consequent: Audibility of absolute or relative phase difference
findings.quote: people are sensitive to neither absolute nor relative phase difference between various components of the periodic stimulus if the components are separated in their frequencies by more than one critical band.

findings.antecedent: Spectral envelope and temporal envelope of sound
findings.quote: Two physical factors are commonly mentioned as physical correlates of timbre: the spectral envelope and the temporal envelope of the sound.

findings.antecedent: Sound duration (after onset, for continuous sound)
findings.quote: it takes at least 60 ms to recognize the timbre of continuous sound after its onset.

findings.antecedent: Sound character (e.g., timbre, spaciousness, roughness)
findings.quote: Sound character is expressed on scales from more to less, while sound quality is expressed on scales from better to worse.

findings.antecedent: Pleasant events
findings.quote: pleasant events appear to last shorter (time contraction) and unpleasant events longer (time dilation) than their actual physical durations.

findings.antecedent: Short acoustic events
findings.quote: In the case of very short acoustic events, humans have a general tendency to overestimate sound duration

findings.antecedent: Short pauses (silent intervals)
findings.quote: short pauses seem to last as much as 2 to 4 times longer than short sound bursts of the same duration

findings.antecedent: Higher frequency of sound (for short pauses)
findings.consequent: Perceptual difference (between perceived and physical duration)
findings.quote: The higher the frequency of the sound, the greater this perceptual difference.

findings.antecedent: Short time gaps (between sequential stimuli, due to forward masking)
findings.quote: In the case of short time gaps when the TE is primarily a result of a forward masking, the TE is positive (+TE).

findings.antecedent: Long time gaps (between sequential stimuli, due to decaying memory trace)
findings.quote: In the case of long time gaps, when the time error is due to decaying memory trace of the first stimulus, the TE is negative (-TE).

findings.antecedent: Longer temporal gaps (between signals for sound quality assessment)
findings.quote: regardless of whether the judgment is quantitative or qualitative, longer temporal gaps between signals lead to larger variability in listener judgments

findings.antecedent: Unfamiliar foreign language
findings.consequent: Speech perception (special character tied to speech production)
findings.quote: if the speech sounds are unfamiliar to the listener (e.g., listening to an unknown foreign language), the speech looses its special character caused by coupling between speech perception and speech production of the listener

findings.antecedent: Noisy environments (Lombard effect)
findings.consequent: Talker's voice (vowel duration, intensity, fundamental frequency, spectral envelope)
findings.quote: the Lombard effect... a phenomenon in which a talker alters his or her voice in noisy environments. Generally, there is an increase in vowel duration and voice intensity

findings.antecedent: Lombard effect
findings.consequent: Speech intelligibility in a noise environment
findings.quote: signal processing techniques that replicate the Lombard effect improve the intelligibility of speech in a noise environment

findings.antecedent: Lower speech test complexity / Quieter background noise
findings.quote: As the speech test complexity gets lower and the background noise gets quieter, the SRT decreases.

findings.antecedent: Contextual information (in speech material)
findings.quote: Speech intelligibility performance generally improves as the material becomes more complex and contains more contextual information and higher degree of redundancy

findings.antecedent: Trained talker / Clear speech
findings.quote: A trained talker such as radio announcer who speaks clearly will be more intelligible than a talker using normal conversational speech.

findings.antecedent: Female voice
findings.quote: a female voice is generally more intelligible than a male voice

findings.antecedent: Trained listeners / Familiarity with test and speech material
findings.quote: Trained listeners who are familiar with the test and the speech material to be tested will perform best and have the most reliable scores

findings.antecedent: Impaired hearing
findings.quote: Listeners who have impaired hearing will perform differently than normal hearing counterparts, even if the average intensity levels are above threshold

findings.antecedent: High SNRs (15-30 dB)
findings.quote: Good understanding of speech requires high SNRs in the order of 15 to 30 dB.

findings.antecedent: Noise levels (up to 85 dB SPL, with sufficient SNR)
findings.quote: As long as the SNR is sufficiently high to allow enough of the speech signal to be heard in the noise, the absolute level of the noise has a minimal effect on speech understanding as long as the noise levels are below 85 dB SPL.

findings.antecedent: Random, unpredictable noise / Speech-like noise
findings.consequent: Informational masking (in addition to energetic masking)
findings.quote: random, unpredictable noise, or noise where the temporal and spectral characteristics are similar to that of speech, can add informational masking to the energetic masking.

findings.antecedent: Reverberation
findings.quote: An acoustic environment can also add reverberation to the speech signal. Reverberation consists of multiple reflections of the sound that mask the direct sound.

findings.antecedent: Spatial configuration of speech source and noise sources (separated in space)
findings.quote: If the two signals are separated in space, binaural cues can be used to separate the two locations, and the listener can selectively attend to the target speech signal.

findings.antecedent: Familiarity with the original signal and surrounding space (for monaural cues)
findings.consequent: Sound localization ability (vertical plane, front-back axis)
findings.quote: sound localization ability, especially in the vertical plane and along the front-back axis, improves with experience and familiarization with both the stimuli and environment

findings.antecedent: Listener moves head while sound is present
findings.consequent: Auditory system's ability to gain disambiguating information (localization)
findings.quote: Even if a sound is unfamiliar, the auditory system can gain disambiguating information if the listener moves his or her head while the sound is present

findings.antecedent: Second sound delayed up to ~30-40 ms (precedence effect)
findings.quote: the perception of the second of two successively received similar sounds is suppressed if the second sound is delayed up to about 30 to 40 ms

findings.antecedent: Lagging sound >10-15 dB more intense than leading sound (precedence effect)
findings.quote: if the lagging sound is more than 10 to 15 dB more intense than the leading sound, only the second sound and its direction are heard

findings.antecedent: Distance to sound source
findings.quote: In general, people underestimate the distance to the sound source in an exponential manner – the larger the distance to the sound source the larger relative error
